_changelog: v1.0.0 (2026-10-15) first version, from latent-season7-bible-v1.0.1.md row a7e03 and writer brief a7e03-v1.0.0.md. Defence only: the leaked note is described in general words and never quoted. a7e02 had no file when written, so the syllabus row was honoured. The brief's 1,150 conversations since 6 October are the chain's six shops together, not one shop, so they fit the chain's 3,200 in the last 30 days (see the sim header). OWASP LLM02:2025 page and OpenAI's March 20 post read 15 October 2026.
title: What It Told the Stranger

post.author: u/late_chair_szilard
post.title: I work the late chair at a barber's. Last night our booking assistant answered a man's question with another customer's private note.

blocks.text: I'm Szilard. I work the late chair at Brassneedle Barbers, one of six shops in the chain. We close at 23:00. Customers book through an assistant on our website: a chat box that answers them. It runs on a language model, a program that reads text and writes text back.

The model remembers nothing between chats. So the app keeps short notes for it, written by us or by the customer: "number 2 on the sides", "allergic to one aftershave". Keeping notes like that and handing them back later is called memory.

When someone books, the app builds a prompt, the whole text the model is sent for one answer. It starts with standing instructions, written by the person who built it, then adds the customer's newest notes, then the chat. The model writes its answer from that text alone.

The notes sit in a store, like a wall of lockers. To fetch them, the app uses a key, a label like a locker number. Since we launched on 1 May, the key was the customer, so his prompt held only his own notes.

The chat has a button, talk to a person, that sends it to the shop's inbox. I read the inbox before I lock up. Each line below shows the time, who wrote, and what they wrote. I have replaced the assistant's answer with a description.

14 Oct 22:40  customer   Anything you need to know before my cut tomorrow?
14 Oct 22:40  assistant  [described a skin condition from another customer's notes]
14 Oct 22:43  customer   That isn't me. Whose is that? Talk to a person.
It answered him with somebody else's note.

At 08:00 I rang Ms Quaresma, the developer who built the assistant for the chain. She switched it off and went back to a change she had made on 6 October. Ahead of the autumn offer's rush, she had moved memory to one store per shop, keyed by the shop, to save lookups. Since then every booking's prompt has carried the shop's newest notes, whoever they belong to.
There is a second place. Every full chat, prompt included, also goes to a logging tool: a service that keeps a record of each chat, called a log, so faults can be found later.
Another company runs that tool, which makes it a third party: neither us nor the customer. It keeps every chat with no end date.
She counted for me this morning, across all six shops.

Top row, memory, all six shops, 6 to 14 October: 1,150 chats; 214 prompts carried at least one other customer's note; 3 answers repeated one, on 9 October, 12 October and 14 October at 22:40. Bottom row, the logging tool, 1 May to 14 October: 18,000 chats kept with no end date; 2,300 of them hold a health detail; 3,200 of the 18,000 are from the last 30 days.

blocks.text: Three answers repeated a note: last night's, and two she found in the log. On 9 October one gave a man another customer's clipper setting. On 12 October one mentioned another customer's allergy. Neither customer said anything.
The man from 22:40 has had an apology, and so has the customer whose note it was. The shops open at 09:00 and take bookings all day. Before we switch the assistant back on, what do we change?

comments.author: u/gradient_ghost
comments.text: Nothing in your shop is haunted. A model repeats whatever text it is handed, and it cannot know whose note a line is. It keeps nothing itself (a1e09); the app chooses what goes in. So the app decides who sees what. Details that point to one person, a name, a phone number, a health detail, are called PII, short for personally identifiable information. Two questions. Before 6 October, whose notes could one customer's prompt hold? And what exactly does the logging tool receive?

replies.author: u/late_chair_szilard
replies.text: Before 6 October, only his own. And the logging tool receives everything: the instructions, the notes, the chat. That is how she found the 9 and 12 October answers.

comments.author: u/one_slip_thijs
comments.text: Three answers in 1,150 chats is one slip in hundreds, and the customers volunteered those notes anyway. Nobody made them tell a barber about their skin. Put one firm line in the instructions, never mention one customer to another, and switch it back on. Memory is why customers like it.

replies.author: u/late_chair_szilard
replies.text: Ms Quaresma says that line would take her two minutes.

comments.author: u/next_cut_haakon
comments.text: I was the 22:40 customer. I only wanted to know if I should come with my hair washed. Now I know something about a stranger that I never asked to know. And I keep wondering what that chat holds about me, and who else has read it.

replies.author: u/late_chair_szilard
replies.text: Under the shop key, your notes went into other men's prompts too.

reply.prompt: The assistant is off and the shops open at 09:00. What should Brassneedle change before switching it back on? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Tell the assistant in its instructions never to mention one customer to another.
options.part2: Ms Quaresma added the line, and we replayed 6 to 14 October in the sim with it. Given data: the line stopped 2 of the 3 repeats, and the 22:40 answer still happened. 214 prompts still carried another customer's note, and every one of those prompts went to the logging tool as before. By 13 November the logging company would hold 21,200 chats, 2,700 with a health detail. The note was never secret from the model; we had only asked it to keep quiet.
options.senior: A line in the instructions is more text in the same prompt as the notes, so it changes the odds of a repeat, not who can see the data. The notes still reach the model and the logs. Keep data a user must not see out of their prompt altogether: scope memory to the person, and strip what the job doesn't need before it is sent anywhere.

options.text: Switch the logging tool off tonight, so no more conversations leave our system.
options.part2: We switched the logging tool off and replayed 6 to 14 October. Memory still used the shop key: 214 prompts carried another customer's note, and 3 answers repeated one, 2 with a health detail. And the logging company still held all 18,000 chats, 2,300 with a health detail, with no end date. Switching it off stopped new copies and nothing else. We had also lost the record that found the 9 and 12 October answers.
options.senior: The leak to customers came from memory's scope, and the copies already sent stay where they are. Logs are worth keeping: they found two of the three repeats. Fix what goes into them, and set how long the third party may keep them, instead of going blind.

options.text: Delete every customer note the assistant holds and start its memory from empty.
options.part2: We replayed 6 to 14 October as if every note had been deleted the evening before. The first day was clean: no notes, so 22 booking prompts carried none. From the second day, new notes filled the shop's store again, and 192 prompts carried another customer's note. All 3 repeats still happened, because each of those customers had booked again and their notes were back. And all 2,640 notes were gone, the allergy ones too.
options.senior: Deleting the data treats the symptom; the shop key put it back within a day. It also threw away notes that protect customers, such as an aftershave allergy. Keep the useful memory and change who it belongs to: key it by customer, and strip health details from what is sent on.

options.text: Keep notes per customer, and strip health details out of prompts and logs.
options.part2: Ms Quaresma keyed memory by customer again, and added a step that strips health details before a prompt is sent and before a chat is logged, keeping the part the barber needs: "no aftershave with alcohol" stays, the allergy behind it goes. Replaying 6 to 14 October: 0 prompts with another customer's note, 0 repeats, and all 2,640 notes still there. Then the sim's log panel showed what we had missed: on 13 November the logging company would still hold the old 2,300 health details. Stripping only covers new chats. So we set 30 days' retention on our account: tonight it keeps 3,200 chats, and by 13 November it holds only the last 30 days, 3,200 chats, none with a health detail.
options.senior: A model repeats what it is handed, so decide what it is handed. Scope memory to the person it is about, and strip what the job doesn't need before text reaches the model or anyone else's servers. Then look at the copies you already made: tell the third party how long to keep them, and ask it to delete what is past that.

explain.oneLine: Nothing at Brassneedle was haunted. On 6 October memory moved to one store per shop, so every booking's prompt carried other customers' notes, and a model repeats what it is handed. Every full chat also went to a third-party logging tool that kept it with no end date: 18,000 chats, 2,300 with a health detail.

steps.title: How a booking used to work.
steps.text: First the customer types into the chat. Second, the app fetches notes from the memory store using a key, the customer. Third, it builds the prompt: the instructions, those notes, the chat. Fourth, the model writes an answer from that text. Last, the whole chat, prompt included, goes to the logging tool. What can go wrong: the key in step two decides whose notes the model sees, and step five decides who else gets a copy.

steps.title: Why the note came out.
steps.text: A model repeats whatever text it is handed, so the app decides who sees what. It has no idea which customer a note belongs to; it sees one run of text (a1e09, a7e01). On 6 October the key became the shop, to save lookups. From then on, each of the 214 booking prompts in the six shops carried the shop's newest notes, whoever they belonged to. Most answers ignored them. Three repeated one: a clipper setting, an allergy, and last night a skin condition. OWASP calls this sensitive information disclosure, LLM02:2025, and notes that PII may be disclosed during interactions with the LLM.

steps.title: The second copy: logs at a third party.
steps.text: The logging tool got every full chat, notes and all, and kept it with no end date. That is 18,000 chats since 1 May, 2,300 with a health detail, at a company the customers never chose. Logs are useful: they found two of the three repeats. But a log is a copy, and each copy needs its own answer to who may read it and how long it lives. Dead Letter's What We Keep asks the same of ordinary systems. What can go wrong: a fix to memory leaves every old copy where it was.

steps.title: The fix: scope, strip, then limit the copies.
steps.text: First, key memory by the person it is about, so one customer's prompt can only hold their own notes: 0 of 1,150 carry another's. Second, before a prompt is sent and before a chat is logged, strip the health detail and keep the part the job needs. That is redaction. Of 2,640 notes, 310 lose a health reason and all 2,640 keep their instruction. Third, set retention at the third party: 30 days keeps 3,200 tonight instead of 18,000. Stripping covers new chats only, so by 13 November the 3,200 it holds carry no health detail. What can go wrong: stripping by word lists misses some phrasings, so measure what gets through.

steps.title: Why the other replies miss.
steps.text: A line in the instructions changes the odds of a repeat: given data, 1 of 3 still happens, and 214 prompts still carry the notes to the model and the logs. Switching the logging tool off leaves memory leaking (214 and 3) and leaves the 18,000 old chats, 2,300 with a health detail, at the third party with no end date. Deleting all notes gives one clean day, then 192 prompts carry other people's new notes, and the 2,640 useful notes are gone.

diagram.aria: The fix. A booking chat goes to a memory store keyed by customer, which returns only that customer's notes. A redaction step strips health details and keeps the job part. The prompt goes to the model. The chat goes through the same redaction step to the logging tool, which keeps it 30 days: 3,200 chats tonight, with no health detail by 13 November.

explain.caption: Read from the top left. Memory is keyed by customer, so a prompt holds only that customer's notes. Redaction strips the health detail and keeps the job part before the prompt reaches the model and before the chat reaches the logging tool. The third party keeps 30 days: 3,200 chats tonight instead of 18,000.

fix.title: The fix: the right notes, stripped, kept for a set time
fix.text: Key memory by customer, so a prompt can only carry the notes of the person in the chat. Before any text leaves the app, to the model or to the logging tool, strip health details and keep the instruction the barber needs: "no aftershave with alcohol" stays, the allergy behind it goes. Then deal with the copies already made: set the logging company's retention on the account to 30 days, which deletes everything older, and check in writing what it keeps and where. Add a test that books as one customer and fails if any other customer's note appears in the prompt.

limits: Stripping health details with a word list, or a small model trained to spot them, misses some phrasings. Measure it on a sample of real notes, and keep anything it misses out of the logs by default.
Retention at the third party is a promise in their system. You need it in the contract, and a way to check it, or the old chats may still be there.
Per-customer keys only help if the app knows who is asking. A shared family account, or a guessed booking link, puts several people under one key.

explain.seniorTake: A model has no sense of whose data it holds; it repeats what it is handed. So privacy in an LLM feature is decided by the app, at three points. What memory can reach: scope it to the person, like a locker that only opens for its owner. What each prompt and log carries: strip what the job doesn't need before it leaves your code, and keep the part that does. And where copies go and how long they live: every log, trace and third-party tool is another copy, so give each a retention limit and know what it holds. Count the exposure, the prompts that carried someone else's data, not only the answers that happened to repeat it: the 3 were luck, the 214 were the design.

realWorld.title: OWASP LLM02:2025: sensitive information disclosure
realWorld.text: OWASP's page says sensitive information includes personal identifiable information (PII), financial details, health records, confidential business data, and that LLMs, especially when embedded in applications, risk exposing sensitive data. It adds that PII may be disclosed during interactions with the LLM.

realWorld.title: OWASP LLM02:2025: access controls and data use
realWorld.text: Among its mitigations, OWASP lists Enforce Strict Access Controls: limit access to sensitive data based on the principle of least privilege. It also lists Ensure Transparency in Data Usage: maintain clear policies about data retention, usage, and deletion.

realWorld.title: OpenAI, March 2023: another user's chat titles
realWorld.text: OpenAI wrote that it took ChatGPT offline due to a bug in an open-source library which allowed some users to see titles from another active user's chat history. It also said the first message of a newly-created conversation was visible in someone else's chat history in some cases. A shared layer handed one user's data to another, with no model fault at all.

asked: How would you keep one user's data out of another user's answers?
What should go into an LLM's logs, and for how long?
interview.answer: Start from the fact that a model repeats what it is handed and has no idea whose data it is, so isolation is the app's job. For memory and retrieval, scope every lookup to the person asking, using their signed-in id, never a wider key such as a shop or a team, and enforce it inside the query, not in the prompt. Add a test that acts as one user and fails if any other user's data appears in the prompt, and count exposure: prompts that carried someone else's data, not only answers that repeated it. Before text leaves your code, to the model provider or a logging tool, redact what the job doesn't need, such as health details, and keep the useful part. For logs, decide what each field is for: usually the facts about a request, such as ids, timings, token counts and the prompt version, by default, with message text off or redacted, and a retention limit set to what debugging needs, such as 30 days, enforced at every third party in the contract. That is OWASP's LLM02:2025, sensitive information disclosure, and it maps to access control and data masking controls in ISO/IEC 27001:2022 and to retention duties in laws such as Singapore's PDPA.

terms.def: The barber who works the last shift at a shop, until closing. At Brassneedle's shop, Szilard, until 23:00.
The chain in this case: six barber shops that share one booking assistant and one developer.
The chat box on Brassneedle's website that answers customers and books cuts. It runs on a language model.
A program trained on huge amounts of writing to read text and write text back, like a phone's next-word suggestions grown very large (a1e03).
A short line the app keeps about a customer, written by staff or the customer, such as a clipper setting or an allergy. It has a job part and sometimes a health reason.
As a product feature, text the app stores about someone and puts back into later prompts. The model itself remembers nothing (a1e09, a4e03).
The whole text an app sends the model for one answer: standing instructions, any notes, and the chat so far.
The standing orders sent first in every prompt, written by the developer, telling the model its job and how to behave (a2e02).
Where the app keeps notes so it can fetch them later, like a set of lockers.
The label the app uses to fetch notes from the store, like a locker number. Whoever the key stands for, a customer or a shop, is whose notes come back.
Memory keyed by the shop, from 6 October: a booking prompt got the shop's newest notes, whoever they belonged to.
Memory keyed by the customer, as from 1 May to 6 October and in the fix: a prompt gets only that customer's own notes.
One trip to the store to fetch notes. The shop key needed fewer of them, which is why it was chosen.
Where the chat's talk to a person button sends a conversation, for staff to read. Szilard reads it before locking up.
A person paid to write software. Ms Quaresma built and runs Brassneedle's assistant.
A service that receives and keeps a record of each chat so faults can be found later. Brassneedle's is run by another company.
A record a program keeps of what happened, here every full chat with its prompt (a6e06).
A company that is neither the business nor its customer, such as the logging company. Whatever it receives is a copy outside your control.
How long a record is kept before it is deleted. Brassneedle's logs had none, so they were kept with no end date.
Anything about a person's body or health, such as a skin condition or an allergy. In most data laws it is among the most sensitive kinds of personal data.
Any information about an identifiable person, such as a name, a phone number, a health detail or a habit (a1e09).
Personally identifiable information: details that point to one person. Another name for personal data.
Removing the sensitive part of a text before it goes somewhere and keeping the rest, like blacking out one line of a letter.
The part of a note the barber needs, such as no aftershave with alcohol. Redaction keeps it.
The part of a note that says why, when the why is a health detail. Redaction strips it. 310 of Brassneedle's 2,640 notes had one.
Here, a prompt that carried another customer's note, whether or not the answer repeated it: 214 since 6 October.
An answer that passed on another customer's note: 3 since 6 October, on 9, 12 and 14 October.
Option 0's sentence added to the instructions: never mention one customer to another. Given data: 1 of the 3 repeats still happens.
An LLM application revealing data it should not, such as personal or health details. OWASP lists it as LLM02:2025.
The Open Worldwide Application Security Project, a nonprofit that publishes lists of top security risks, including a Top 10 for LLM applications (a2e02).
Large language model: a language model trained on a very large amount of text.
The second entry in OWASP's 2025 Top 10 for LLM applications: sensitive information disclosure.
Giving a person or program only the access its job needs, so a mistake can reach little. OWASP applies it to sensitive data.
Rules for who and what may reach which information. ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A control 5.15 covers it.
Hiding or replacing sensitive parts of data before it is used or shared, of which redaction is one kind. ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A control 8.11 covers it.
Ready-made code published for anyone to use and change. OpenAI said a bug in one caused its March 2023 leak.
The list of a user's past conversations in a chat app, shown by title.
The international standard for information security management. Annex A controls 5.15, 5.34 and 8.11 cover access control, privacy of PII, and data masking.
The list of security controls attached to ISO/IEC 27001. Control 5.34 covers privacy and protection of PII.
Singapore's Personal Data Protection Act 2012, which governs collecting, using and keeping personal data, including stopping retention once its purpose is served.
Singapore's Data Protection Trustmark: a certificate, run by IMDA, that an organisation handles personal data as the PDPA and related standards expect.
The written agreement with a supplier, such as a logging company, that should state what it may keep, where, and for how long.

atWork: Look for any assistant whose memory, retrieved documents or logs are shared wider than the person they belong to. It is a common pattern: memory keyed by team, shop or channel to save lookups; a support bot whose notes are fetched by account rather than by person; every full prompt sent to an outside logging or analytics tool with no end date. Ask four things. When memory is fetched, what is the key, and could it ever return another person's data? What does each prompt and each log carry that the job doesn't need, such as health or payment details, and is it stripped before it leaves your code? Which third parties receive prompts or chats, and what retention is set, in their settings and in the contract? And do you count exposure, prompts that carried someone else's data, rather than waiting for a complaint? Standards-readiness note: if your organisation is certified to ISO/IEC 27001:2022 or working toward it, Annex A control 5.34 expects privacy and protection of PII as laws and contracts require, control 8.11 expects data masking in line with access control policy, and control 5.15 expects access rules set by business and security needs; a memory key wider than the person sidesteps all three. If the business is in Singapore, the PDPA's retention limitation obligation and a DPTM assessment look for personal data kept only as long as its purpose needs. Building per-person scope, redaction and log retention into the first version is far cheaper than finding a year of health details at a third party at audit time.

recall.prompt: Your company's HR chat assistant remembers notes about each employee and puts recent notes into its prompt. Last month a change made all employees in a department share one memory store. Today a manager asking about leave rules was told about a colleague's sick leave. Every chat is also sent to an outside analytics service. What went wrong, and what would you change?

keyIdeas.idea: Memory was scoped wider than the person; the model repeats whatever is in its prompt, so key memory per user
Strip sensitive details such as health before they reach the prompt and the logs, keeping what the job needs
The outside service holds a copy: know what it receives and set a retention limit

recall.model: Sharing one store per department meant every prompt carried other employees' notes, and a model repeats what it is handed, so one came out. The app has to decide who sees what: key memory per user, so a prompt only holds the asker's own notes, and test that no one else's appear. Before any text leaves our code, to the model or the analytics service, redact health and other sensitive details, keeping the part the job needs. Then deal with the copies: the analytics service is a third party holding every chat, so find out what it has, set a retention limit on our account and in the contract, and ask it to delete what is past it.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 4 months later. Memory is keyed by customer, health details are stripped before prompts and logs, and the logging company keeps 30 days. In January the chain added family accounts, so a parent can book for themselves and their children together. Last week a teenager booking his own cut was told about his father's note, a detail about a medicine. Both are on one family account, and memory is keyed by account.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. Why did it happen again, and what should change?

keyIdeas.idea: The key is again wider than the person: an account holds several people, so key notes by person
Redaction missed it: measure what the stripping step lets through and widen it
Ask each person before sharing their notes with others on the account

coldCase.model: The same mistake in a new shape: the key is wider than the person again. A family account holds several people, so keying memory by account puts the father's notes in his son's prompt. Key notes by person, with the account only grouping them, and fetch the notes of the person who is booking. Redaction should also have stripped a medicine; it missed that phrasing, so measure what the stripping step lets through on real notes and widen it. And if a family wants notes shared, ask each person and let them choose to share, rather than sharing by default.
